verdict.plain_answer_for_student:
Short version: keep the topic, but change the question. As you pitched it ("a digital PLL across radios, running on the GPU, so cheap crystals replace GPSDOs"), it has been done since 2012. AirSync, MegaMIMO, Chorus (LTE, 2018) and Merlo & Nanzer (2025, 2-4 USRPs, no cables) all do it. Jiang et al. (2026) already track inter-radio phase from uplink SRS every TDD period on NR-style hardware. Doing it on a GPU is a choice of platform, so it does not make the work new. Any examiner will cite these papers within a minute.

Phase-locking a GPU to a CPU would do nothing for 5G. The carrier phase that ruins coherent transmission lives in each radio's crystal and RF PLL, not in any compute clock. Drop that idea.

There is a real, live problem where crystals and PLLs hurt 5G and 6G. 3GPP added coherent joint transmission (CJT) across several sites in Rel-18 assuming perfect sync. Rel-19 then had to add UE reports of phase and frequency offset because sync is not perfect. Cao et al. (IEEE JSAC 2023) measured commercial O-RAN radios locked with PTP+SyncE. Each radio's own PLL still drifted more than 20 degrees in 7.5 ms, and multi-user spectral efficiency fell 46% with 5 ms calibration delay and 64% with 10 ms. Their own remark says the drift comes from each radio's PLL and that LO phase tracking is future work.

The question nobody has answered on hardware is this: is that PLL drift predictable over the 1.5 to 4 ms you have to look ahead in an O-RAN/GPU baseband, so that software tracking can fix it? Or is it fast PLL noise that only better PLL hardware can fix? Where does the answer flip as carrier frequency rises from 3.5 GHz to the 7-15 GHz bands 6G is targeting?

You can answer this in weeks, with 3 USRPs or with no hardware at all. Either outcome is a result, and it uses exactly your crystal/PLL/timing interest. The GPU is still part of it, because it is where the loop would sit in a real DU and where you run the large simulations. It is not the novelty, though, and you should not claim it is. This will not single-handedly transform 5G. It is a narrow, honest, testable contribution on a problem that 3GPP and operators name as a blocker. That is what a strong MSc thesis, or a workshop or conference paper, looks like.
verdict.novelty_honest:
These parts are NOT new:
- Estimating per-radio phase and frequency offsets from pilots, tracking them with a PLL or Kalman filter, and pre-rotating each radio's precoder. AirSync 2012 (Kalman, FPGA), MegaMIMO 2012, MegaMIMO 2.0 2016, Chorus 2018 (LTE), Rogalin 2014, Quitin/Madhow 2013.
- Cable-free coherent USRP arrays. Merlo/Nanzer 2025: 60-70 ps, >99% median coherent gain.
- Kalman LO tracking inside the NR-style TDD frame. Ngo & Larsson 2025/26, in simulation.
- Per-TDD-period UL-SRS phase tracking with COTS RRUs. Jiang et al. 2026 at 26 GHz; Cao et al. 2023 measured the drift.
- UE-reported inter-TRP phase, frequency and delay offsets. Rel-19 TS 38.214 5.2.1.4.9-11, cjtc-Dd/F/P.
- Running the loop on a GPU. The arithmetic is tiny (under 2 GFLOP/s for 4 TRPs), so a CPU can do it.

What appears open (from the four reports plus my own spot checks of Cao, Jiang and Merlo, and two web searches; still check this with your supervisor):
(1) An experimental answer on whether inter-radio LO drift under a shared frequency reference can be predicted at the O-RAN weight-computation horizon (about 1.5-4 ms). All existing work either assumes a model (Wiener) or reports one operating point. Cao's Remark 2 attributes the drift to the radio PLL and leaves tracking as future work.
(2) A head-to-head of network-side SRS prediction against Rel-19 CJTC UE reports (24 or 11.6 degree phase steps, 0.39-13.3 ppb frequency steps, plus CSI latency). No public comparison was found.
(3) The carrier frequency at which the residual after an ideal slot-rate loop is set by the synthesizer's PLL phase noise rather than by tracking. That gives a PLL specification for 6G FR3 (7-24 GHz) CJT.

This is an incremental, measurement-driven contribution, not a new paradigm. The evidence does not support calling it revolutionary.
verdict.the_specific_question:
For multi-user coherent joint transmission, radios share a frequency reference (PTP/SyncE-like) but each has its own LO PLL. The DU must fix precoders about 1.5-4 ms before air time (O-RAN 7.2x / Aerial FAPI 3-slot advance plus the TDD/SRS period). Two questions follow.

(a) What fraction of the measured inter-radio carrier-phase drift can a second-order predictor (type-II DPLL or 2-state Kalman fitted to the oscillator's Allan deviation) remove, compared with simply holding the last SRS estimate?

(b) As carrier frequency rises (3.5 -> 7 -> 13 GHz), at what point does the residual stop being limited by tracking and start being limited by the radios' own PLL synthesizer phase noise? In other words, what PLL/oscillator specification would 6G FR3 CJT radios need to keep residual phase error at or below about 5 degrees (the multi-user ZF requirement)?

Use the Rel-19 CJTC UE-report quantisation and latency as the standards baseline.
verdict.why_it_matters_5g:
Rel-18 CJT (up to 4 TRPs, FR1) assumed ideal sync. Rel-19 NR_MIMO_Ph5 added "CJT with non-ideal synchronization" via UE reports, which shows the problem is real and only partly addressed. PTP/SyncE aligns time to tens of ns. That is about 1260 degrees of carrier per ns at 3.5 GHz, so PTP cannot align carrier phase.

On commercial PTP+SyncE O-RAN radios, Cao et al. measured +/-30 degree LO wander, more than 20 degrees within 7.5 ms, and a 46%/64% multi-user spectral-efficiency loss at 5/10 ms calibration delay. Systems work such as RANBooster (SIGCOMM 2025) assumes PTP-synced RUs are coherent enough.

Ericsson/Nokia authors (Shafi et al. 2025) and XGMF 2026 name phase-synchronous downlink as a main reason D-MIMO adoption is slow. A measured answer to "can DU-side prediction fix this, or must the RU PLL be better?" bears directly on whether TDD CJT can rely on network-side tracking, which needs no 3GPP change, instead of UE reports that industry calls undesirable.

The size of the effect is in multi-user ZF: the SINR ceiling is about 15 dB at 10 degrees and about 21 dB at 5 degrees. In single-user beamforming it is small: 30 degrees costs about 0.5-1 dB.
verdict.why_it_matters_6g:
The 6G Radio study (RP-251881) requires reusing the 3.5 GHz site grid at about 7 GHz with comparable coverage, which pushes toward more antennas and cooperative or distributed MIMO. No inter-TRP sync mechanism has been agreed in 6GR, and the RAN1 CSI discussions mention "uncalibrated radios and phase errors" while still using the Rel-18 CJT codebook as baseline. Normative specs come in Rel-21 (about 2027-28), so evidence produced now can still matter.

Phase drift per ppb scales with carrier frequency: 1.26 deg/ms at 3.5 GHz, about 2.5 at 7 GHz, about 4.7 at 13 GHz, 10 at 28 GHz. Synthesizer jitter also scales, roughly with 20log(fc). The kill-test model already puts the ideal-loop floor near 6.5 degrees at 13 GHz and about 10 degrees at 28 GHz, where ZF rate falls to about 0.89 of ideal.

For 6G FR3 distributed MIMO, the question therefore shifts from "better software tracking" to "how good must each radio's PLL and reference be". That is a quantitative hardware-specification result linking crystals and PLLs directly to a 6G design decision.

first_experiment.what: Measure whether the inter-radio carrier-phase drift between two independently synthesised radios sharing one 10 MHz reference can be predicted 1.5-4 ms ahead. Hold-last-SRS is compared with a type-II DPLL and with a 2-state Kalman filter, replayed offline on the real phase trace, and the residual is turned into a multi-user ZF loss. There is a $0 no-hardware fallback on digitised Cao et al. traces.
steps: Day 1: ask your supervisor or lab manager for 3 USRPs (B210/B200/X310) and a way to share 10 MHz (OctoClock or a signal generator plus a splitter). Also get 2x 30 dB attenuators, a 2:1 combiner and SMA cables. Check that each B210 is one TRP, because its two channels share an LO.

Wire it cabled, with no over-the-air link and no licence needed: TX-A and TX-B go through the attenuators into the combiner and then into RX. Case S: TX-A and TX-B take the shared 10 MHz (and PPS). Case F: both run on internal TCXOs, as a control. The RX may use its own clock, because its LO cancels when you take the phase difference.

Open each device as a separate UHD multi_usrp in Python and tune once to 3.5 GHz (repeat later at 5.8 GHz if possible). Never retune during a run, because AD9361 LO phase re-randomises on retune. TX-A sends a CW tone at +100 kHz baseband and TX-B at -100 kHz. Use narrowband (1 MSps or less) so that sample-clock offset does not matter.
Record 3 x 10 minutes per case. Note room temperature, and do one run with a deliberate disturbance (a fan on the boards).

Offline (numpy, laptop): for each 0.5 ms block, take the phase of each tone bin and form psi(t) = phi_A - phi_B. Unwrap it, remove the mean frequency, and compute the Allan deviation and phase PSD from 1 ms to 10 s.

Replay: sample psi at SRS periods {2.5, 5, 10, 20} ms with measurement noise added at 20 dB SNR. Predict ahead by h in {1.5, 2.5, 4} ms with (a) hold-last, (b) an alpha-beta / type-II DPLL with a bandwidth sweep, and (c) a 2-state Kalman with Q fitted to the measured ADEV. Record the residual rms for each method.

Extend the existing killtest.py (4 TRPs, 2-4 UEs, RZF). Feed it the measured residuals and report the multi-user ZF SINR ceiling and the rate ratio against ideal. Sanity anchor: feed it a Cao-like trace (+/-30 deg wander, >20 deg per 7.5 ms) and check that it reproduces a 40-65% loss at 5-10 ms delay.

Fallback if no USRPs: digitise Cao et al. Fig. 8a/8b and Jiang et al.'s tracking plots (WebPlotDigitizer, from arXiv 2208.14048 and 2601.14648) and run steps 6-7 on those traces. Say clearly that this is coarse.
first_experiment.metric: Residual rms inter-radio phase error (degrees) at prediction horizon h = 1.5 / 2.5 / 4 ms for hold-last vs DPLL vs Kalman, and its conversion to the multi-user ZF SINR ceiling (about -20log10(sigma_rad) dB) and RZF rate ratio against ideal. Secondary: relative Allan deviation and phase PSD of psi in case S (a small public dataset in itself), and the measured CFO in case F.
first_experiment.success_looks_like: In case S, hold-last at h = 2.5 ms gives 10 degrees or more, and the DPLL/Kalman predictor cuts it at least 2x, to 5 degrees or less. That lifts the ZF ceiling from about 15 dB or less to about 21 dB or more, and the rate ratio from 0.9 or less to 0.97 or more. The predictor's advantage grows with h. The drift is then predictable, DU-side tracking is the fix, and you go on to the Sionna study and the Rel-19 CJTC comparison.
first_experiment.failure_looks_like: (i) Hold-last is already 3 degrees or less at 4 ms. The B210 PLLs under a shared reference are much quieter than Cao's commercial RRUs, so the problem does not reproduce on this kit. Rely on the Cao-calibrated model, try X310/UBX or different LO settings, and state the hardware dependence. (ii) The predictor is no better than hold-last (within about 10%) and the PSD is flat over the 100 Hz-1 kHz range. The drift is fast PLL-loop noise that no slot-rate loop can remove, so the fix is the RU's PLL or clock-cleaner design, not software. That is a publishable negative result, and you pivot to question (b): a PLL specification for FR3 CJT. (iii) Case F shows kHz-level CFO and fast slips. That only confirms frequency discipline is mandatory and is expected; do not treat it as the result.
first_experiment.cost_and_time: About 3 weeks. 2-3 days to set up and get the UHD script working, 1 day to record, 1-2 weeks for analysis and the replay/ZF model. Cost is $0 if the lab has 3 USRPs and a 10 MHz source, plus about $100-300 for attenuators, a combiner and cables. Buying 3 B210s would cost about $7k, which is out of budget, so use the fallback instead. No GPU is needed for this step. The fallback (digitised Cao/Jiang traces) costs $0 and takes about 1 week.

later_experiments: Sionna (PyTorch, Sionna 2.2 has no oscillator block, so write a ~50-line per-TRP exp(j*theta_n(t)) block): 38.901 UMi/InH, N = 2/4/8 TRPs x 4 antennas, K = 2-8 UEs, RZF downlink built from generic OFDM blocks. The oscillator model is fitted to your measured ADEV plus a PLL phase-noise term (not a pure Wiener process, which overstates PLL-locked drift by more than 10x). Report sum SE against prediction horizon and SRS period. About 2-10 GPU-hours on vast.ai, $1-15.

Standards baseline: implement Rel-19 CJTC quantisation (cjtc-P M = 16/32, cjtc-F 0.1/0.2 ppm with M = 16/32/256, cjtc-Dd) with realistic CSI-report latency (5-20 ms). Compare it with network-side SRS prediction on the same traces. Check the formulas against the official TS 38.214 v19.x, including the sign convention for FO.

FR3 crossover (6G): repeat at 7, 13 and 28 GHz with numerology 30/60/120 kHz. Scale the reference noise by 20log(fc/fref) and use PLL datasheet models (e.g. TI LMX2594 FOM, ADI ADF4372). Find the minimum synthesizer integrated jitter and reference ADEV that keep the residual at or below 5 degrees at a 2.5 ms horizon. The output is a 'required PLL spec vs carrier' curve.

Close the loop on hardware: RX feeds psi-hat and f-hat back over Ethernet, TX-B pre-rotates (digitally or via the UHD DSP NCO), and both transmit together. Measure coherent gain against the ideal 3 dB, and ZF null depth at a second RX. Null depth is the sensitive metric: about -15 dB at 10 degrees.

Multi-UE pooling: the TRP oscillator term is common to all UEs' SRS, while Doppler is per UE. Test whether a pooled per-TRP estimator separates TRP drift from UE motion and allows longer SRS periods. Avoid cycle slips with a 2-symbol DMRS/TRS frequency-acquisition step.

GPU integration, presented honestly: fuse the per-TRP tracker into a batched SRS->RZF PyTorch/CUDA module and measure the added latency at 64-256 ports. If an Aerial cuPHY testbed with 2+ RUs becomes available, insert it into the SRS-BFW pipeline. Claim zero added latency, not that the GPU is needed for the loop.
verdict.what_it_can_and_cannot_prove:
It CAN show, for the specific radios measured, whether inter-radio LO drift under a shared frequency reference can be predicted at O-RAN-relevant horizons, and how much multi-user ZF performance a second-order predictor recovers compared with hold-last and with Rel-19 UE-report quantisation. With the FR3 extension it can give a quantitative, model-based PLL/oscillator specification for CJT at 7-28 GHz.

It CANNOT prove:
- that the result transfers to commercial O-RAN RUs. USRP/AD9361 PLLs differ from RRU clock trees, and Cao's drift was 10-20x the idealised model, so state the hardware dependence.
- end-to-end 5G-stack gains. OAI and srsRAN cannot do multi-TRP CJT with independent radios, and there is no Aerial multi-RU testbed.
- mobility, multipath robustness of OTA/SRS estimation, or scaling past about 4 radios.
- that cheap free-running crystals can replace PTP/SyncE. At 3.5 GHz a 0.5-2 ppm TCXO gives 1.75-7 kHz CFO (6-23% of a 30 kHz subcarrier). That causes ICI a DU-side frequency-domain rotation cannot remove, and TS 38.104 requires +/-50 ppb anyway.
- anything about GPU necessity. The loop is cheap enough for a CPU.
biggest_risks: Hardware is unconfirmed. Without 3 USRPs and a shared 10 MHz source, the distinctive measured part becomes a digitised-trace or simulation study, which reviewers may read as a rerun of Ngo & Larsson or BeamSync.

Unrepresentative hardware. B210 PLLs under a shared reference may drift far less (or differently) than commercial RRUs, which would leave nothing to fix on your kit. Mitigation: report it, and anchor the simulation to Cao et al.'s measured +/-30 deg and >20 deg per 7.5 ms.

Prior-art crowding. Any wording like 'novel digital PLL across radios' or 'GPU makes coherence possible' will be rejected; keep the claim to the predictability measurement, the Rel-19 comparison and the FR3 PLL-spec curve.

Model mistakes. A pure Wiener phase model overstates ms-scale drift for PLL-locked carriers by more than 10x. 3GPP TR 38.803 pole-zero models have no close-in drift and understate it. Either mistake makes the simulation meaningless.

Measurement artefacts. AD9361 LO phase re-randomises on retune. TX and RX use separate synthesizers, so reciprocity is not guaranteed. Sample-clock offset matters in free-running runs. Cycle slips occur at long SRS periods (80 ms) and with XO-class oscillators at FR3.
Weak metric choice. Single-user coherent gain hides the effect (30 degrees costs about 0.5-1 dB); always report multi-user ZF SINR, rate or null depth.

Standards details come partly from secondary mirrors (iTecSpec, ShareTechnote, summaries). Verify the CJTC formulas, RP numbers and the TS 38.104 TAE and frequency-error values against the official 3GPP/ETSI documents before quoting them in the thesis.
verdict.if_not_this_then:
If no radios are available and the student wants to stay in simulation, do question (b) on its own: "What PLL and reference-oscillator specification do 6G FR3 (7-24 GHz) distributed-MIMO radios need for multi-user CJT under O-RAN latency, and when is a shared LO or reference unavoidable?" Combine datasheet PLL models (FOM, loop bandwidth, reference ADEV) with Cao-calibrated drift, run GPU Monte-Carlo sweeps in Sionna ($1-15), and compare with Rel-19 CJTC quantisation. It keeps crystals, PLLs, timing and GPUs, needs no hardware, and gives a concrete spec curve, though it is weaker than a measured result.

A second fallback: publish a small open dataset of inter-USRP carrier-phase drift (free-running, shared 10 MHz, shared 10 MHz with disturbances, over 1 ms to 10 min). Published measured traces are scarce (only isolated plots in Cao 2023).

Do not pursue: GPU-to-CPU phase locking (no effect on RF coherence), or "cheap crystals with no shared reference in NR" (physically limited by CFO and ICI under split 7.2).

key_findings: VERDICT: the core idea is NOT novel. It is about 14 years old. Estimating each radio's phase and frequency offset from pilots, tracking it with a filter (Kalman or PLL-like), and rotating each radio's precoder so independent oscillators add coherently at the receiver is the central mechanism of AirSync (2012), MegaMIMO/JMB (2012), MegaMIMO 2.0 (2016), Chorus (2018, LTE), Rogalin et al. (2014) and Merlo & Nanzer (2025). Running that loop on a GPU is a platform choice, not a scientific contribution. As stated, the proposal is INCREMENTAL at best. A narrower version that is NR-specific and measurement-driven still has a defensible gap (see what_is_open).

MegaMIMO / JMB (Rahul, Kumar, Katabi, SIGCOMM 2012; the brief says 2013 but it is 2012; 'JMB' and 'MegaMIMO' are the same paper): 10 USRP2 APs with independent oscillators, 10 clients, 2.4 GHz. One lead AP; each slave estimates its oscillator rotation relative to the lead from a sync header and corrects it before joint transmission. Result: 95th-percentile phase misalignment of 0.05 rad (2.86 deg) and about 10x throughput with 10 APs. Needs no shared clock, only Ethernet backhaul. Not real-time (host processing).

AirSync (Balan, Rogalin, Michaloliakos, Psounis, Caire; MobiCom 2012 / IEEE-ACM ToN 2013): a master broadcasts an out-of-band pilot tone, and slaves track the phase drift with a Kalman predictor and correct the carrier phase across the transmit slot. Implemented as a digital circuit in the WARP FPGA. Phase coherence 'within a few degrees', timing within the OFDM cyclic prefix, testbed of 2 to 4 APs. Needs a dedicated receive antenna or chain for the pilot tone. A Kalman-predicted phase loop across distributed radios on cheap hardware was therefore demonstrated in 2012.

MegaMIMO 2.0 (Hamed, Rahul, Abdelghany, Katabi, SIGCOMM 2016): the first real-time, fully distributed 802.11n D-MIMO PHY, on Zynq Z7020 FPGAs with AD FMCOMMS2 front ends, 4 APs x 2 antennas, 2.457 GHz, 20 MHz. No shared clock. Extends reciprocity to independent oscillators and finds that AGC gain changes can flip phase by up to pi rad. Throughput up to 3.3x (330%). The paper says plainly that industry CoMP 'assumes a shared clock, distributed either via GPS or a wire'.

Chorus (Hamed, Rahul, Partov, SIGCOMM 2018): leaderless D-MIMO in which all nodes contribute to the sync signal. It scales past single-hop range, is described as 'the first scalable distributed MIMO system for LTE', is 3GPP-LTE compatible with unmodified UEs, and runs real-time on FPGA. It reports 2.7x throughput over leader-based sync. Cellular-standard-compatible distributed phase sync with independent oscillators has therefore existed since 2018.

Related wireless-reference systems: Vidyut (Yenamandra & Srinivasan, SIGCOMM 2014) distributes a reference tone over power lines (claims 8.2x over MegaMIMO). AirShare (Abari, Rahul, Katabi, Pant, INFOCOM 2015) broadcasts two tones whose difference is a shared clock. RFClock (Alemdar et al., MobiCom 2021) is an open-source wireless 10 MHz/PPS leader-follower board with mean frequency offset <0.107 Hz and time/phase within 5 ns, tested in a 5-node distributed coordinated beamforming setup. All three need extra RF hardware or a reference channel.

Merlo, Wagner, Lancaster, Nanzer (MSU/LLNL, arXiv 2506.07267, 2025) is the closest prior art to the student's USRP plan. It does fully digital, real-time wireless time, frequency and phase calibration of 2 to 4 COTS Ettus X310 USRPs on their own internal references: no cables, no GNSS, two-way time transfer, processing on host CPUs. Results: about 60-70 ps time/phase precision at 27 dB SNR, median coherent gain >99%, 3.73 ppb frequency RMSE under motion, at 1.0 and 2.1 GHz carriers. A companion paper (arXiv 2506.13014) reports 2-node collaborative comms up to 256-QAM over 58 m with mean coherent gain 0.936. Both are non-NR waveforms. Their stated limitation is that host CPUs miss real-time deadlines and the work should move to FPGA. Reproducing 'cheap oscillators + 2-4 USRPs + digital loop' would repeat this work.

Larsson group (Linkoping/Ericsson), mostly theory and simulation. Rogalin et al. (IEEE TWC 2014) covers scalable sync and reciprocity calibration for distributed MU-MIMO with 802.11-grade clocks. BeamSync (Ganesan, Sarvendranath, Larsson, IEEE TWC 2024) derives optimal OTA phase and frequency offset estimators that beamform sync signals between APs, with no fronthaul measurements and simulation only. Larsson & Vieira (2023) covers phase calibration of distributed arrays. 'Massive Synchrony' (Larsson, IEEE TSP 2024) shows calibration error can grow without bound with network size for some topologies, and that one global calibration is optimal. Ngo & Larsson (GLOBECOM 2025; arXiv 2509.03722v2, May 2026) builds inter-AP OTA phase measurements into the TDD flow by shifting UL/DL switch points, adds a KALMAN FILTER for LO phase tracking, and derives spectral efficiency for conjugate and ZF beamforming, in simulation only. A repeater-aided OTA phase sync scheme (Ganesan, Thoota, Larsson, arXiv 2603.19903, 2026) reaches about 1e-3 rad RMSE in simulation. A 'Kalman phase tracking across distributed APs' contribution is therefore already published in theory.

Southeast University / Purple Mountain / China Mobile, the closest 5G-NR prior art. Cao et al. (IEEE JSAC 2023, arXiv 2208.14048): a cell-free prototype with 4 COTS O-RAN split-7.2 RRUs x 4 antennas, 4 UEs, 4.9 GHz, 100 MHz, OTA reciprocity calibration using SRS-like reference signals in the NR S-slot, with RRUs locked to PTP+SyncE. Even with that common reference, each RRU's LO phase wandered about +/-30 deg and drifted >20 deg within 7.5 ms. A calibration delay of 5 ms / 10 ms cost 46% / 64% of sum spectral efficiency (16 streams, ZF). Their Remark 2 names LO phase tracking as the way to cut overhead. Jiang et al. (arXiv 2601.14648, Jan 2026): 4 TRPs and 2 UEs at 26 GHz, 200 MHz, still PTP+SyncE, with bidirectional OTA calibration plus CALIBRATION-PHASE TRACKING FROM THE UE's UL SRS EVERY TDD PERIOD and sensing-assisted tracking for dynamic scenes. Without tracking the error stays >90 deg; with tracking it falls below 20 deg, and overhead drops to about 10%. 'Per-slot SRS-based inter-TRP phase tracking to pre-compensate CJT precoding' is therefore published for NR-like systems with COTS RUs.

3GPP: Rel-18 introduced CJT across multiple TRPs, extending the Type-II codebook. Rel-19 (frozen in 2025) adds CJT 'with non-ideal synchronization and backhaul such as inter-site CJT', with UE measurement and reporting of inter-TRP time misalignment and frequency/phase offset (sub-7 GHz, FDD and TDD). Industry patents already cover UE-assisted inter-TRP calibration and time-domain phase tracking for multi-TRP CJT. The standard is moving toward UE-assisted calibration, so network-side SRS phase tracking is the TDD complement, not a new paradigm.

Shared-reference approaches (the incumbent): O-RAN fronthaul requires PTP+SyncE (the LLS-C1/C3 S-plane). NVIDIA Aerial cuPHY (Release 26.3 docs) depends on PTP/SyncE and contains only per-UE PUSCH CFO estimation from DMRS. The docs contain no inter-RU phase calibration and no CJT, so a GPU-native inter-RU phase loop does NOT exist in Aerial. White Rabbit (Bigler, Treytl, Loschenbrand, Zemen, ISPCS 2018) gives sub-ns time and ps-level precision over fiber for D-MIMO; the same paper computes that about 0.8 ps is needed for phase-accurate arrays at 5 GHz. Analog radio-over-fiber CJT (Puerta et al., EuCNC 2023) shows +5 dB combined gain with 2 TRxPs by distributing coherence over fiber. Ericsson radio stripes carry fronthaul, power and sync in one daisy-chained cable. REINDEER/RadioWeaves uses the Techtile testbed with PTP-disciplined 10 MHz/PPS per tile, and near-field WPT beamfocusing reached 14 dB vs 14.9 dB theoretical with 31 elements; phase errors below 20 deg cost under 1 dB, above 40 deg over 3 dB.

RANBooster (Microsoft Research / UC Berkeley, SIGCOMM 2025) builds dMIMO from commodity O-RAN RUs by remapping antenna ports in a fronthaul middlebox. It ASSUMES the needed phase sync is 'guaranteed' because RUs are PTP-synchronised. Cao et al.'s measurements contradict that: PTP+SyncE RUs drift >20 deg within 7.5 ms. This is a concrete, citable gap between systems practice and the PHY literature.

Distributed ISAC: MovISAC (arXiv 2502.08236, 2025, simulation at 26.5 GHz / 400 MHz, 2-4 devices) does OTA sync from the LOS path with about 0.1 deg phase std. 'Over-the-Air Time-Frequency Synchronization in Distributed ISAC' (arXiv 2503.08920) uses scatterers as sync media. Lohuis, Hardeveld, Klumperink (Twente) derive targets of 3.3 ppb and 4 ps for cooperative ISAC radio units with crystal oscillators, reachable with millisecond-scale OTA resync. Doppler-only D-MIMO ISAC (arXiv 2609.19401) sidesteps phase coherence. Long-term coherence on real hardware is still largely untested.

Learning-based work: GNN-aided OTA reciprocity calibration for cell-free (Sun, Mu, Wu, Ouyang, Liu, IEEE WCL vol. 15, 2026). Deep reciprocity calibration for mmWave massive MIMO (IEEE TWC 2024, co-located arrays). Robust beamforming under time-evolving 'residual calibration error' combining phase mismatch, residual CFO and phase noise (Sun et al., arXiv 2608.10637, 2026). Differential STBC/modulation to avoid phase alignment altogether (Freitas, Buzzi, Interdonato, arXiv 2503.04935). Adding a neural network to the tracker is also already being explored.

Experimental OTA vs local calibration (Collmann, Nimr, Fettweis, arXiv 2605.22384, 2026, USRP X310 arrays): both remove phase drift, but OTA calibration is sensitive to multipath and channel conditions. This is a known weakness of any pilot-based inter-radio loop.

Tooling check: NVIDIA Sionna 2.2.0 (cloned and grepped) has NO built-in oscillator phase-noise or CFO impairment block. The phrase appears only in tutorial text. The student would have to write the Wiener/PLL phase-noise and per-node CFO models themselves, which is easy but must be validated against real oscillator data.
numbers: MegaMIMO 2012: 10 USRP2 APs, independent oscillators, 95th-percentile phase misalignment 0.05 rad (2.86 deg), about 10x throughput with 10 APs, 2.4 GHz.
AirSync 2012: phase coherence 'within a few degrees', timing within the OFDM CP, WARP FPGA, 2-4 APs, Kalman-predicted phase drift.

MegaMIMO 2.0 2016: 4 APs x 2 antennas (8x8 virtual MIMO), Zynq Z7020 + FMCOMMS2, 2.457 GHz / 20 MHz, up to 3.3x throughput. AGC gain steps can introduce up to pi rad phase change, and uncorrected phase errors cap SNR at about 12-14 dB.
Chorus 2018: LTE-compatible, leaderless, 2.7x over leader-based D-MIMO.
RFClock 2021: frequency offset <0.107 Hz mean, time/phase within 5 ns, 5-node beamforming.
Merlo/Nanzer 2025: 2-4 COTS X310s, no cables/GNSS, about 60-70 ps time/phase std at 27 dB SNR, median coherent gain >99%, 3.73 ppb frequency RMSE under motion, carriers 1.0 and 2.1 GHz.

Cao et al. JSAC 2023: 4 COTS O-RAN RRUs, 4.9 GHz / 100 MHz, PTP+SyncE-locked. LO phase wander about +/-30 deg, >20 deg drift in 7.5 ms. 5 ms calibration delay puts 5% of channels above 10 deg error; 10 ms puts 10% above 15 deg. Sum-SE loss 46% (5 ms) and 64% (10 ms) for 16-stream ZF.

Jiang et al. 2026: 4 TRPs, 26 GHz / 200 MHz. Without phase tracking the error is >90 deg; SRS-based tracking brings it below about 20 deg (at about 30 dBm calibration power); calibration overhead cut to about 10%.
Repeater-aided OTA sync (2026, simulation): about 1e-3 rad RMSE at 30 m with a 10 mW repeater. At 3 GHz, 0.01 rad corresponds to 0.5 ps.
White Rabbit D-MIMO (Bigler 2018): sub-ns accuracy, ps precision. About 0.8 ps is needed for phase-accurate arrays at 5 GHz, and about 33 ps for 0.01 m/s velocity accuracy.
ARoF CJT (EuCNC 2023): +5 dB combined diversity and power gain with 2 TRxPs.
Techtile WPT: 14 dB measured vs 14.9 dB theoretical for 31 elements. Phase error <20 deg costs <1 dB; >40 deg costs >3 dB.
CJT tolerance (inter-cell calibration study, arXiv 1905.01046): pi/8 (22.5 deg) gives trivial loss, pi/4 is acceptable, pi/2 gives clear degradation.
Twente cooperative ISAC targets: 3.3 ppb frequency stability and 4 ps time error, reachable with crystal oscillators at millisecond-scale OTA resync intervals.

My own budget (3.5 GHz, 30 kHz SCS, 0.5 ms slot; script at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/c22b0607-07f1-5108-a24d-4caf6e85f472/scratchpad/phasesync/budget.py): XO +/-10 ppm gives 35 kHz CFO (1.17x the subcarrier spacing; OFDM breaks, so digital phase correction alone cannot fix it). XO 2 ppm gives 7 kHz (0.23 SCS, ICI-limited SIR about 7.5 dB). TCXO 0.5 ppm gives 1.75 kHz (315 deg per slot, ICI SIR about 19.5 dB, not enough for 256-QAM). OCXO 10 ppb gives 35 Hz (6.3 deg per slot). Free-running crystals therefore need frequency locking (OTA, SyncE or two-tone), or time-domain pre-compensation at the radio, before any per-slot phase loop helps.

Coherent-gain loss for i.i.d. Gaussian residual phase error sigma (large N approximation e^-sigma^2): 10 deg costs 0.13 dB, 20 deg 0.53 dB, 30 deg 1.19 dB, 45 deg 2.68 dB. Monte Carlo with N=4: 0.10, 0.39 and 0.86 dB at 10, 20 and 30 deg. Single-user coherent combining is forgiving. Multi-user ZF is not: a crude leakage ceiling is about 1/sigma^2, roughly 15 dB SINR at 10 deg and 9 dB at 20 deg. That is why the Cao et al. losses are tens of percent.
what_is_already_solved: Digital phase and frequency tracking across distributed radios with independent oscillators, using a lead or reference signal plus filter prediction and pre-rotation of each radio's transmit signal: AirSync 2012 (Kalman, FPGA), MegaMIMO 2012, MegaMIMO 2.0 2016 (real-time), Chorus 2018 (LTE, leaderless).

Fully digital, cable-free, GNSS-free coherent distributed arrays on 2-4 COTS USRPs with >99% coherent gain and about 60-70 ps precision (Merlo & Nanzer 2025). The student's 'optionally on 2-4 USRPs' plan would replicate this.
Kalman-filter LO phase tracking for distributed MIMO with OTA inter-AP measurements built into the NR-style TDD frame, with SE analysis for CB and ZF (Ngo & Larsson 2025/2026, theory and simulation).

Optimal OTA phase and frequency offset estimators between APs (BeamSync, TWC 2024), scalability analysis (Massive Synchrony, TSP 2024), repeater-aided extension (2026), map/location-assisted wideband phase and time calibration (Wu, Keskin, Gustavsson, Seco-Granados, Larsson, Wymeersch, arXiv 2410.23120).

OTA reciprocity calibration with COTS 5G O-RAN RRUs in NR S-slots, plus UL-SRS-based per-TDD-period calibration phase tracking for coherent joint transmission and sensing at sub-6 GHz and 26 GHz (Cao et al. JSAC 2023; Jiang et al. 2026).
Standards path for CJT with non-ideal inter-TRP sync, using UE-reported time misalignment and frequency/phase offset (3GPP Rel-19).
Shared-reference alternatives: PTP+SyncE (O-RAN S-plane), White Rabbit, analog RoF, radio stripes, wireless two-tone references (AirShare, RFClock, Nanzer CWTT), power-line references (Vidyut).
Non-coherent fallbacks that avoid phase sync: differential STBC and differential modulation for cell-free (2025).
what_is_open: A REAL-TIME, NR-compliant inter-RU phase-tracking loop inside a GPU DU (Aerial cuPHY or OAI on GPU) for COTS split-7.2 O-RAN RUs. Aerial has no inter-RU calibration or CJT. RANBooster (SIGCOMM 2025) builds dMIMO from PTP-synced commodity RUs and assumes PTP is enough, while Cao et al. measured >20 deg drift in 7.5 ms on PTP+SyncE RRUs. A 'PTP-only dMIMO vs PTP + SRS phase loop' comparison on real RUs is a concrete, publishable systems gap. The contribution is the measurement plus closing the loop at line rate, not the algorithm.

Calibration aging across SRS-to-PDSCH latency: Cao et al. show 46-64% SE loss at 5-10 ms delay. Predicting the phase forward with a fitted oscillator model (Kalman with Wiener+CFO states, or a PLL-type loop filter), validated on measured RU phase traces, is only analysed in simulation (Ngo & Larsson; Sun et al. 2608.10637). An experimental 'SE vs prediction horizon' curve on real hardware is still missing.

Public measurement datasets of inter-RU / inter-USRP carrier-phase drift under PTP-only, PTP+SyncE and free-running TCXO setups, over ms to minute timescales and temperature. Only isolated plots exist (Cao 2023). RENEW publishes CFO datasets for distributed uplink (Zafari et al., arXiv 2508.08506), but not for downlink CJT phase.

Free-running cheap crystals (no SyncE) in NR numerology: at 3.5 GHz even a 0.5 ppm TCXO gives about 5.8% of a 30 kHz subcarrier as CFO, which causes ICI. With split 7.2 the DU only sends frequency-domain IQ, so a GPU loop can apply per-symbol phase but cannot remove intra-symbol CFO. Making 'cheap crystals' work therefore needs a frequency-transfer or OTA disciplining stage at the RU. That interface (what the DU estimates vs what the RU corrects) is not well specified.

Mobility and multipath robustness of OTA/SRS-based tracking (Collmann et al. 2026 find OTA calibration multipath-sensitive; Jiang et al. needed sensing assistance in dynamic scenes). Scaling past about 4-8 radios on hardware (Larsson's unbounded-error topologies). Interaction with UE-side Rel-19 reports (fusing network-side SRS tracking with UE-reported offsets).
Distributed ISAC long-coherence on hardware: most D-ISAC phase sync work (MovISAC, OTA D-ISAC) is simulation only.
implications: Do NOT pitch this as 'a new digital PLL across radios that lets cheap crystals replace GPSDO/OCXO'. Examiners and reviewers will cite AirSync, MegaMIMO, Chorus and Merlo & Nanzer immediately. The 'GPU' part does not make it novel.

A defensible MSc-scale reframing is a measurement-plus-systems study. (1) Measure inter-radio carrier-phase drift for 2-4 radios under three regimes: shared 10 MHz (baseline), PTP-only (host or White-Rabbit-less), and free-running TCXO. (2) Fit oscillator models (Wiener + CFO + PLL-filtered) to the traces. (3) Feed them into a Sionna/GPU CJT simulation (the student must add phase-noise/CFO blocks; Sionna 2.2 has none) to get SE vs tracking interval and vs prediction horizon. (4) Show that a Kalman/PLL predictor recovers most of the measured calibration-aging loss, quantified against Cao et al.'s 46-64% number. This targets an open experimental gap and fits weeks-to-months on a tens-of-dollars budget.

If lab USRPs exist, the honest novelty margin over Merlo & Nanzer is: NR numerology and SRS/DMRS-based estimation instead of a dedicated two-way time-transfer waveform, multi-user ZF (not just single-target coherent gain), and GPU-side real-time closure at slot rate (0.5 ms). Their own stated limitation is that host CPUs missed deadlines.

If the student wants hardware relevance to industry, the RANBooster/Aerial gap is the sharpest: show quantitatively that PTP-synced O-RAN-style dMIMO loses coherence, and that an SRS-driven per-RU phase correction in the DU restores it. This works directly on the student's cuPHY experience without new RF hardware, provided an Aerial/OAI testbed with 2+ RUs is available, which is not confirmed.

The student's earlier instinct to 'phase-lock a GPU with a CPU' is irrelevant to 5G coherence. Carrier phase lives in each radio's RF LO/PLL reference, not in GPU or CPU clock domains. The useful 'PLL' is a digital loop that estimates RF LO phase from pilots, which is exactly the prior art above.

Expected effect sizes are modest for single-user coherent gain: under 0.5 dB loss at 20 deg residual. They are large for multi-user ZF CJT: tens of percent SE. Frame any claimed improvement around multi-user CJT under realistic tracking latency, not single-user beamforming gain.
red_flags: The brief's 'MegaMIMO (SIGCOMM 2013)' is wrong. It is SIGCOMM 2012, and JMB is the same paper. MegaMIMO 2.0 is SIGCOMM 2016, not MobiCom.
Claiming novelty for 'Kalman phase tracking across distributed APs/TRPs' would be false. It is in AirSync (2012) and Ngo & Larsson (2025/26).

Claiming novelty for 'per-slot SRS-based inter-TRP phase tracking in NR' would be false. Jiang et al. (arXiv 2601.14648, 2026) and Cao et al. (JSAC 2023) do it with COTS O-RAN RRUs, although with PTP+SyncE-locked references.

'Cheap crystals with no shared reference' is physically limited in NR. Free-running XO/TCXO CFOs at 3.5 GHz (1.75-35 kHz) are a sizeable fraction of the 30 kHz subcarrier spacing, so frequency must be disciplined (SyncE, OTA two-tone or two-way transfer) before a slot-rate phase loop can work. With O-RAN split 7.2, the GPU DU cannot apply intra-symbol frequency correction.
Simulation-only results with a Wiener phase-noise model will look like Ngo & Larsson and BeamSync. Without measured oscillator traces or hardware, the contribution will read as a re-derivation.

Sionna 2.2.0 has no phase-noise/CFO impairment model. Any 'realistic oscillator model' must be implemented and justified by the student (for example the 3GPP TR 38.803 multi-pole/zero PN model or measured Allan deviation).
USRP availability is unconfirmed. Without at least 2 radios with independent references, the only distinctive (experimental) part of the plan collapses.

key_findings: THE PROBLEM IS LIVE IN STANDARDS RIGHT NOW. Rel-18 added coherent joint transmission (typeII-CJT-r18: up to 4 TRPs, FR1, per-TRP co-amplitude and co-phase in the PMI) but assumed ideal backhaul and synchronisation (Qualcomm Rel-18 deck: 'coherent-JT for up to 4 TRPs, assuming ideal backhaul and synchronization in sub-7 GHz'). Rel-19 NR MIMO Phase 5 (NR_MIMO_Ph5, unique ID 1020089; WID RP-234007 approved at RAN#102 Edinburgh in Dec 2023 and later revised, per secondary sources) then specifically targeted 'CJT with non-ideal synchronization and backhaul such as inter-site CJT'. The objective was UE measurement and reporting of inter-TRP time misalignment and frequency/phase offset, for FR1 FDD and TDD.

WHAT REL-19 ACTUALLY SPECIFIED (TS 38.214 Rel-19, sections 5.2.1.4.9 to 5.2.1.4.11). There are three new reportQuantity values, each measured on N_TRP 'CSI-RS resource sets for tracking' (one TRS per TRP), with every TRP reported relative to a reference TRP n_ref:
(a) 'cjtc-Dd' delay offset: quantised over [0, A_D), A_D in {CP/2, CP}, M_D in {32, 64, 128, 256} levels, top index = out of range.
(b) 'cjtc-F' frequency offset: FO_n = k_n*A_FO/(M_FO-1), A_FO in {0.1 ppm, 0.2 ppm}, M_FO in {16, 32, 256}, top index = invalid.
(c) 'cjtc-P' phase offset: Phi_n = p_n*2*pi/(M_Phi-1), M_Phi in {16, 32}, wideband or per configured subband (subbandSizeCJTC).
The combined report 'cjtc-Dd-F' also exists. So 3GPP chose UE-assisted measurement and reporting, with compensation left to gNB implementation.

WHAT THE REL-19 REPORTS CAN RESOLVE (my calculations from the spec formulas):
- Phase step: 24 deg (M=16) or 11.6 deg (M=32), so worst-case quantisation error is about +/-12 deg or +/-5.8 deg.
- Delay step at 30 kHz SCS (normal CP = 2343.75 ns): from 4.6 ns (CP/2, M_D=256) to 75.6 ns (CP, M_D=32).
- Frequency step: from 0.39 ppb (0.1 ppm/255) to 13.3 ppb (0.2 ppm/15).
Because the reports travel through the CSI framework (CSI-RS, then UE computation, then PUSCH/PUCCH), the loop runs at CSI-reporting latency (several ms or more). In the ShareTechnote rendering the FO mapping is non-negative only, so the sign convention should be checked against the official spec.

REL-20 5G-ADVANCED (NR MIMO Phase 6, RP-251856, approved RAN#108 June 2025). The published summaries cover CSI-RS frequency-density reduction for 48/64/128 ports, early CSI acquisition, and SRS spanning an S slot plus the next UL slot. None of them lists a further inter-TRP sync objective (Lin, arXiv 2506.11828). At RAN#113 the WI was listed as not yet complete (RP-261985). Nokia's NGA slides (Apr 2024) had flagged 'CJT non-idealities: frequency and timing offset mitigation, cross-TRP phase calibration (TDD)' as a 5G-A direction. The UE-assisted part landed in Rel-19 as CJTC. I found no evidence that a standardised network-side TDD cross-TRP phase calibration was specified.

6G (Rel-20 study). The 'Study on 6G Radio' (RP-251881, RAN#108 Prague, 9-13 June 2025, moderator NTT DOCOMO) lists only generic 'MIMO operation [RAN1, RAN4]'. It has no explicit CJT, distributed-MIMO or inter-TRP sync objective. It does require reuse of the 3.5 GHz site grid at about 7 GHz with comparable coverage, which motivates more antennas and cooperative transmission. TR 38.914 v1.0.0 (scenarios and requirements) was approved at TSG#112 Singapore on 9 June 2026 (RP-261565); WG-level work continues under FS_6G_Radio (TR 38.960). Normative 6G specs come in Rel-21 (about 2027-2028).
6GR CSI discussions at RAN1#124bis-#126 (2026) use the Rel-18 eType-II CJT codebook as the high-resolution multi-TRP baseline. They also discuss 'codebook adaptations for uncalibrated radios and phase errors' and widely-spaced multi-panel. I found no agreed 6GR mechanism for inter-TRP phase/frequency sync, so this is still open for 6G.

WHAT CURRENT SYNC SPECS DELIVER, AND WHY THEY DO NOT ALIGN CARRIER PHASE:
- TS 38.104 BS frequency error: +/-0.05 ppm (50 ppb) for wide-area BS, +/-0.1 ppm for medium-range and local-area BS. Two compliant wide-area sites can therefore differ by up to 100 ppb, which is 350 Hz at 3.5 GHz.
- TS 38.104 TAE: 65 ns for MIMO on a carrier.
- TDD cell phase sync: 3 us (+/-1.5 us).
- Ericsson (Ruffini et al., ETR Jan 2021): the 65-260 ns TAE values apply only to 'colocated/intra-site deployments'.
- O-RAN WG4 (ATIS/Renesas summary of O-RAN.WG4.CUS.0 v14): timing categories A (relative TAE <=130 ns) and B (<=260 ns); regular O-RU |TE| <=80 ns (enhanced <=35 ns); residual fractional frequency offset 21/27/30 ppb (O-DU class A / class B / LLS-C3), or about 13 ppb with a Class B T-TSC and about 3 ppb with Class C.
None of these align carrier phase: 1 ns of time error is 1260 deg of carrier at 3.5 GHz. Carrier-phase alignment therefore has to come from over-the-air measurement (CSI, SRS or calibration signals), never from PTP.

THE STRONGEST QUANTITATIVE EVIDENCE OF THE GAP: Cao et al., IEEE JSAC 2023 (arXiv 2208.14048). The setup was 4 commercial COTS RRUs (4T each), O-RAN eCPRI fronthaul, 100 MHz, with a common PTPv2+SyncE reference but an independent LO PLL per RRU. Findings:
- The calibration-coefficient phase wandered over +/-30 deg even with zero CFO, attributed to each RRU's PLL ('phase drift... relatively large in one frame (10 ms)').
- A 5 ms calibration delay left 5% of channels with more than 10 deg error; at 10 ms, 10% had more than 15 deg.
- Joint-processing RZF spectral efficiency fell by 46% at 5 ms and 64% at 10 ms delay.
- Local (per-RRU) precoding was insensitive to the delay.
The authors explicitly propose 'LO phase tracking' as future work. This is almost exactly the proposed GPU tracking loop, and it shows that commercial PTP/SyncE-synced radios still need sub-10 ms phase tracking for multi-user CJT.

TOLERANCE NUMBERS FOR COHERENT COMBINING (my calculations unless cited):
- Single-user coherent gain is very tolerant. Two TRPs with offset d lose cos^2(d/2): 15 deg costs 0.07 dB and 30 deg costs 0.3 dB. With N TRPs and iid phase error sigma the loss is about exp(-sigma^2): 15 deg costs 0.3 dB, 30 deg costs 1.2 dB.
- Multi-user CJT / cell-free zero-forcing is not tolerant. Leakage caps SINR at roughly 1/sigma^2 (rule of thumb): 21 dB at 5 deg, 15 dB at 10 deg, 11.6 dB at 15 deg. 256-QAM-class SINR therefore needs a few degrees of residual phase error.
- Operator/academic consensus: the XGMF (Japan) Advanced MIMO white paper v2.0 (Apr 2026) says 'In cell-free mMIMO, a phase difference exceeding 15 degrees between antennas is known to impact radio communication quality'; Cao et al. cite the same 15 deg.
- Timing: a delay offset dt is a linear phase ramp across the band. Each 1 ns of residual delay gives 18 deg error at the 50 MHz band edge, so sub-ns residual timing, or per-subband phase, is needed. KTH/Ericsson (arXiv 2305.03189) state D-MIMO needs sub-nanosecond TRxP synchronisation.
- Frequency to phase-drift rate at 3.5 GHz: 1 ppb = 1.26 deg/ms. So 3 ppb = 3.8 deg/ms, 13 ppb = 16.4 deg/ms, 21 ppb = 26.5 deg/ms, 50 ppb = 63 deg/ms, 100 ppb = 126 deg/ms.

WHERE THE LOOP WOULD RUN IN O-RAN 7.2x / NVIDIA AERIAL. In split 7.2x the O-DU high-PHY (cuPHY on GPU) owns SRS channel estimation, beamforming-weight computation and PDSCH precoding; the O-RU does the FFT/iFFT and owns the LO. A per-RU phase/frequency tracker therefore fits inside cuPHY's existing 'SRS-based channel estimation' and 'PDSCH dynamic BFW calculation from SRS channel estimates (regularized zero-forcing)' pipeline. It costs only N_RU complex rotations per symbol/subband, needs no fronthaul or RU change, and needs no 3GPP change, because TDD reciprocity calibration is implementation-specific.
Latency budget: cuPHY sends SLOT.indication 3 slots ahead (FAPI) with a 500 us L2 budget, so weights for DL slot N are fixed about 1.5 ms (3 slots at 30 kHz) before air time. Adding SRS processing and a DDDSU 2.5 ms TDD period, the loop must PREDICT phase about 1.5-4 ms ahead.
Cost of that horizon: at 13 ppb residual FFO, a phase-only (first-order) update accrues about 25-65 deg, which fails for multi-user CJT. A second-order (phase + frequency state, i.e. a digital PLL / Kalman) predictor with about 1 ppb frequency-estimate error accrues about 2-5 deg. That quantitatively justifies the 'digital PLL' framing.
One gap: cuPHY docs list PTRS as unsupported and do not mention CJT or multi-RU joint precoding.

key_findings: Two independent radios' phase error has three separate parts, and a loop that updates once per slot or per TDD period can only fix two of them. (1) A fixed frequency offset gives a straight-line phase ramp. It is large but easy to remove once it is estimated: a loop that tracks both phase and frequency follows it with zero steady-state error. (2) Slow random wander of the reference crystal (flicker and random-walk frequency noise). This is set by the crystal's Allan deviation (ADEV) and is what a millisecond-scale GPU loop can actually fix. (3) Fast jitter, meaning phase noise above about 1/T_update (above ~1 kHz). No slot-rate loop can touch it. It sets a floor of about 0.4 deg (FR1), 3-6 deg (FR2) and 25-45 deg (140 GHz) RMS between two radios in my model.

A simple rule for part (2): if a loop extrapolates the phase linearly between updates spaced tau apart, the RMS phase error between two independent radios is theta_rms(deg) ~ 720 * fc * tau * sigma_y(tau). Here sigma_y(tau) is one radio's ADEV at tau. This follows from Var[second difference of x] = 2 tau^2 sigma_y^2, doubled for two radios. Example: a TCXO with sigma_y(10 ms) ~1e-10 gives about 2.5 deg at 3.5 GHz, 20 deg at 28 GHz and 100 deg at 140 GHz.

Frequency offset alone makes the phase run away fast: 1 ppb of relative offset is 1.26 deg/ms at 3.5 GHz, 10.1 deg/ms at 28 GHz and 50 deg/ms at 140 GHz. If the offset is not estimated, the 3GPP limit of +-0.05 ppm per base station (up to 0.1 ppm between two of them) gives 126 / 1008 / 5040 deg/ms. Two USRP X310 TCXOs (+-2.5 ppm each) give about 6300 deg/ms at 3.5 GHz.

PTP gives each radio a common time, not a common carrier phase. A PTP-only radio has the short-term frequency stability of its own crystal, with only a slow servo correction. So 'PTP only' should be modelled as free-running crystals plus a leftover frequency offset of up to tens of ppb.

SyncE or a shared frequency reference turns the unbounded drift into bounded wander, but not into phase coherence. The best measurement I found: Cao et al. (arXiv 2208.14048), commercial off-the-shelf remote radio units (RRUs) at 4.9 GHz synchronised with IEEE 1588 PTPv2 plus SyncE, saw the phase drift more than 20 deg within 7.5 ms and wander within about +-30 deg over 250 ms. Antennas inside one RRU, which share a local oscillator, stayed within +-1.5 deg. Their conclusion was that the over-the-air calibration signal must be sent often, at least once per 10 ms frame.

Measured hardware drifts about 10-20x more than my idealised model of a TCXO plus an LMX2594-class synthesizer, which predicts about 1 deg at 10 ms at FR1 with SyncE. The difference comes from the radio's own clock-cleaning PLLs and how its reference clock is distributed. Treat the model as a lower bound and measure the real drift on the student's own hardware.

A GPS-disciplined oscillator (GPSDO) fixes long-term frequency (about 1e-11), not short-term phase. Its short-term behaviour is that of its built-in OCXO or TCXO. RFClock (Northeastern University) measured +-500 ns between the pulse-per-second signals of two GPSDOs, and 0-100 ns of relative wander between their clock outputs. That is about 1e5 deg at 3.5 GHz, so GPSDOs alone cannot make two radios phase-coherent.

A chip-scale atomic clock (CSAC) is worse than a good TCXO over the 1 ms to 1 s window that matters here. The SA65 datasheet gives ADEV 3e-10 at 1 s, phase noise of -64 dBc/Hz at 10 Hz and -110 dBc/Hz at 100 Hz, and accuracy at shipment of +-5e-11. It is excellent for long-term frequency but a poor choice for carrier-phase coherence.

Update interval needed to keep the RMS phase error between two radios below 10 / 30 deg (my model, frequency offset tracked, zero latency, hold or linear extrapolation): FR1 3.5 GHz XO 6-20 / 20-52 ms; TCXO 36-78 / 115-206 ms; OCXO ~0.8-1.2 s / >2.6 s; CSAC 2-5 / 6-11 ms. FR2 28 GHz TCXO about 1.6 ms for 10 deg (hold, zero latency; not reached with 1 ms latency) and 13-36 ms for 30 deg; OCXO 64-94 / 250-450 ms; XO never reaches 10 deg and needs about 2-6 ms for 30 deg. At 140 GHz, 10 deg is unreachable with 10 MHz-reference XO/TCXO/OCXO chains in my model: the fast-jitter floor is 25-45 deg. With measured drift (Cao), FR1 hardware needs about 2-5 ms updates, i.e. every TDD period.

Latency matters as much as the update rate. At 28 GHz with a TCXO, 1 ms between measuring and using the estimate raises the error at a 2.5 ms update period from about 11 deg to 16 deg. Jiang et al. (arXiv 2601.14648, 26 GHz cell-free testbed, PTP plus SyncE) measured 0.5 dB loss for joint precoding with a 2-TDD-period (1.25 ms) calibration delay and about 2 dB with 6 periods (3.75 ms).

Single-user coherent combining tolerates phase error well. Loss = -10log10(1/N + (1-1/N)exp(-sigma^2)) for independent Gaussian per-transmitter error sigma. At sigma = 10 deg the loss is 0.07 / 0.10 / 0.12 dB for N = 2/4/8; at 30 deg, 0.55 / 0.86 / 1.02 dB; at 60 deg, 1.76 / 3.01 / 3.80 dB. Fully random phases lose 3 / 6 / 9 dB. For a 10 deg RMS difference between two radios (sigma = 7.07 deg per transmitter) the loss is 0.03-0.06 dB; for 30 deg (sigma = 21.2) it is 0.29-0.52 dB. For N = 2 with a fixed phase difference delta, the loss is -20log10(cos(delta/2)): 0.03 dB at 10 deg, 0.30 dB at 30 deg, 1.25 dB at 60 deg, 3 dB at 90 deg.

Multi-user precoding (zero-forcing / null-steering) is far more sensitive. Rough interference ceiling per leaking stream: SIR ~ exp(-s^2)/(1-exp(-s^2)), i.e. 21 dB at 5 deg, 15 dB at 10 deg, 9 dB at 20 deg, 5 dB at 30 deg. So 10 deg is plenty for single-user combining, but multi-user joint transmission at high-order modulation needs about 5 deg or better. That is the regime where the update rate becomes the binding constraint at FR2.

Typical carrier phase noise (single radio, my LMX2594-class model with 10 MHz references): FR1 3.5 GHz TCXO -91 / -99 / -104 / -131 dBc/Hz at 1k / 10k / 100k / 1M Hz offset, OCXO -99 / -104 / -109 / -134. FR2 28 GHz TCXO -73 / -81 / -86 / -89, OCXO -81 / -86 / -91 / -94. 140 GHz OCXO -67 / -72 / -77 / -80, which is pessimistic: state-of-the-art D-band PLLs report about -108 dBc/Hz at 10 MHz and -121.6 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz. Integrated jitter per radio from 1 kHz to 10 MHz: 0.29 / 0.16 deg at FR1 (TCXO/OCXO), 4.5 / 2.5 deg at FR2, 22 / 13 deg at 140 GHz. The USRP X310 datasheet gives 1.0 deg RMS at 3.5 GHz and 1.5 deg at 6 GHz.

The 3GPP TR 38.803 29.55 GHz pole-zero model (PSD0 = 32, Fp = [1 Hz, 1.6 MHz, 30 MHz], Fz = [3 kHz, 0.55 MHz, 280 MHz], az = [2.37, 2.7, 2.53], ap = [3.3, 3.3, 1], as used by MATLAB nrPhaseNoise) evaluates to -67 / -87 / -97 / -99 / -109 dBc/Hz at 1k / 10k / 100k / 1M / 10M Hz offset, about 2.2 deg RMS per radio over 1 kHz-10 MHz. The 'Model A' set at 30 GHz (PSD0 = -79.4, Fp = [0.1, 0.2, 8] MHz, Fz = [1.8, 2.2, 40] MHz, all exponents 2) is flat at about -79.5 dBc/Hz below 10 kHz, 2.8 deg integrated. These models describe phase noise within a symbol (common phase error and inter-carrier interference, corrected via PT-RS). They have no close-in random-walk or flicker term, so on their own they cannot represent drift from one slot to the next between radios.

A pure Wiener (free-running VCO) model taken from the 100 kHz level badly overstates millisecond-scale drift for a carrier locked to a crystal by a PLL. Linewidth beta = 2*pi*f^2*10^(L/10): -100 dBc/Hz at 100 kHz gives beta = 6.3 Hz and an RMS walk of 11.4 deg per radio after 1 ms, versus about 0.5 deg in the PLL plus TCXO model. Ngo and Larsson (arXiv 2509.03722) use a Wiener model with S100 between -120 and -80 dBc/Hz. That is fine for free-running local oscillators, but the student should not use it for PLL-locked radios without a reference-dominated close-in model.

Sionna 2.2.0 (I downloaded and searched the source) has no phase-noise, frequency-offset or oscillator model. The only mention is a sentence in the MIMO_OFDM_Transmissions_over_CDL tutorial. A custom block is needed: apply exp(j*phi_n(t)) per TRP, either to the time-domain channel or per OFDM symbol to the frequency-domain channel response (a common-phase approximation, fine at FR1). MATLAB 5G Toolbox nrPhaseNoise implements the TR 38.803 (29.55 / 45 / 70 GHz) and TR 38.808 set1/set2 pole-zero models (no FR1 model) and works as a cross-check.

The standard already covers part of this. 3GPP Rel-19 TS 38.214 defines UE reporting for coherent joint transmission calibration (CJTC) of delay offset (5.2.1.4.9, range CP/2 or CP with 32-256 levels), frequency offset (5.2.1.4.10, range 0.1 or 0.2 ppm with M = 16/32/256 levels, resolution 0.39-13.3 ppb) and phase offset (5.2.1.4.11, 2*pi/(M-1) with M = 16 or 32, i.e. 24 deg or 11.6 deg steps, quantisation RMS about 6.9 or 3.4 deg). Even the finest frequency step (0.39 ppb) corresponds to 0.49 deg/ms at FR1 and 3.9 deg/ms at FR2, so a report is stale after a few milliseconds at FR2 unless it is refreshed or tracked in between.

3GPP Rel-18 introduced coherent joint transmission (CJT). Rel-19 TS 38.214 5.2.1.4.9-11 standardised UE reporting of delay, frequency and phase offsets between TRPs for CJT calibration (CJTC-Dd/F/P).

Turning phase noise into Allan deviation and power-law (h_alpha) oscillator models is textbook frequency-metrology material (IEEE Std 1139; Rubiola). Leeson's model and the FOM-based in-band noise of PLL synthesizers are standard.
what_is_open: Realistic simulation models for phase drift between TRPs from one slot to the next. The 3GPP models cover only phase noise within a symbol and are flat close in. Published distributed-MIMO studies mostly use a single Wiener process. There is no open model that combines reference random-walk and flicker FM, the PLL transfer, and SyncE/PTP disciplining, calibrated against measured COTS drift (e.g. Cao's >20 deg per 7.5 ms). Neither Sionna nor 3GPP provides one.

FR2 multi-user CJT with TCXO-grade radios. My numbers put it right at the edge: 10 deg needs updates every 1.6 ms or less with near-zero latency, and multi-user precoding needs about 5 deg. Prediction that accounts for latency (a Kalman filter whose prior comes from oscillator physics, plus a frequency state) and choosing the update rate to fit TDD/SRS opportunities is a narrow open question with numbers attached.

How network-side continuous estimation (from SRS/DMRS, on the GPU) compares with the Rel-19 UE-reported CJTC-P/F quantisation (24 or 11.6 deg phase steps, 0.39-13.3 ppb frequency steps) and its reporting delay. I found no published head-to-head comparison.

Whether reciprocity holds when TX and RX use separate synthesizers (e.g. USRP SBX/UBX daughterboards, the AD9361). Phases measured on the uplink may not apply to the downlink without a calibration after every retune. Cao found the phase between antennas inside one RRU stable, but the general case for cheap radios is less clear.

At sub-THz frequencies, whether any slot-rate loop can work, or whether a shared reference or LO (RF-over-fiber, a wireless reference tone) is unavoidable. In my model fast jitter alone gives 25-45 deg between two radios. This is model-dependent, so I would treat it as an open hardware question rather than a settled one.
implications: FR1 (3.5-4.9 GHz) phase drift is a solved, low-difficulty tracking problem. Given a decent frequency estimate, updating once per TDD period (2.5-5 ms) is plenty, even against the drift measured on commercial hardware. A project that only shows 'the GPU PLL restores coherent gain at FR1' would mostly reproduce Cao 2022 and Ngo-Larsson 2025, so it is not revolutionary.

If the student keeps this direction, FR2 (24-30 GHz) with TCXO-grade radios and multi-user CJT is the regime where the numbers are tight. The contribution could be a latency-aware predictor and update-rate scheduler with a quantified 'error vs SRS period vs latency' curve, compared against the Rel-19 CJTC-P/F UE-report baseline.

Choose the metric carefully. Single-user coherent gain hardly moves: 30 deg RMS costs only about 0.5-1 dB at N = 2-8, so a 'coherent gain recovered' plot will look unimpressive. Multi-user SINR / interference leakage (15 dB ceiling at 10 deg, 5 dB at 30 deg) is the metric where a better tracking loop shows a visible difference.

Simulation recipe for Sionna, which has no built-in support: per TRP n, phi_n(t) = 2*pi*fc*eps_n*t + phi_ref,n(t) + phi_HF,n(t). eps_n ~ U(+-50 ppb) for PTP-only, or about 0 for SyncE. phi_ref is generated by spectral synthesis from the reference L(f) scaled by 20log(fc/fref) inside the PLL bandwidth, or from h_-2/h_-1 values fitted to datasheet ADEV. phi_HF comes from the TR 38.803 pole-zero model at FR2 or an LMX2594-style FOM model at FR1. Apply it per OFDM symbol as a common phase per TRP (FR1) or in the time domain (FR2). Validate against MATLAB nrPhaseNoise and against the 720*fc*tau*sigma_y rule.

For a USRP experiment: two X310s on internal TCXOs drift about 6300 deg/ms relative to each other at 3.5 GHz, so the loop must estimate frequency explicitly. Run three cases: free-running, shared 10 MHz reference (RFClock saw a residual of about 0.2 ppb), and shared 10 MHz with deliberately injected wander. Measure the drift directly first; that alone is a useful dataset because published measured data is scarce.

A GPU is not required for the arithmetic. Estimating phase and frequency for 2-8 TRPs per TDD period is tiny compared with LDPC or channel estimation. The GPU matters only because the loop sits inside the cuPHY/Aerial pipeline, where the latency term (estimate to precoder) has a large effect at FR2. Present it that way rather than as 'a GPU PLL'.
red_flags: The direction is crowded with prior art: Ngo and Larsson 2025/26 (Kalman over-the-air phase tracking in the TDD flow), Cao 2022 and Jiang 2026 (real COTS RRU testbeds at 4.9 and 26 GHz), Merlo (wireless calibration of time, frequency and phase), RFClock, BeamSync, AirSync, Chorus, MegaMIMO, and 3GPP Rel-19 CJTC UE reporting. Calling it 'revolutionary' would be an overclaim. It is an incremental systems or measurement contribution at best.

My model numbers depend on assumptions: a 10 MHz reference, LMX2594-class FOM, PLL bandwidth of 200 kHz (FR1) or 1 MHz (FR2+), and typical rather than datasheet-guaranteed reference phase noise for XO/TCXO/OCXO. Measured COTS drift (Cao) is about 10-20x worse at FR1. The 140 GHz results are pessimistic compared with state-of-the-art D-band PLLs. Use the tables for orders of magnitude, not as final numbers.

The 3GPP TR 38.803 parameters I evaluated (Fp1 = 1 Hz) come from secondary sources (arXiv 2412.05841 and MathWorks), not the TR itself. The '65 ns MIMO TAE' and the G.8262 MTIE wander values are from memory and unverified. Check them against the original documents before quoting.

A Wiener-only phase model, as in Ngo-Larsson style analyses, applied to PLL-locked radios would overstate millisecond-scale drift by more than 10x. 3GPP pole-zero models alone would understate it, because they have no close-in drift. Either mistake would make the simulation results meaningless.

Combining-loss results assume independent Gaussian errors and ideal channel knowledge. Channel aging from UE mobility, delay and timing offsets (which need delay estimation per subband, cf. CJTC-Dd) and reciprocity mismatch between TX and RX chains are not included and may dominate in practice.

The CSAC and GPSDO 'upgrades' do not solve carrier-phase coherence. CSAC short-term stability is worse than a TCXO, and two GPSDOs wander tens of ns relative to each other. Any proposal arguing 'cheap XO plus tracking replaces GPSDO/CSAC' has to make the comparison on short-term phase, where GPSDO and CSAC were never the right baseline.

key_findings: Sionna can model this, but you have to add the oscillators yourself. I checked the Sionna 2.2.0 source (now PyTorch, torch>=2.9.1). It has no phase-noise, CFO or oscillator model: grepping sionna.phy for phase noise, frequency offset and oscillator finds nothing. You add one with about 50 lines that multiply each TRP's channel by exp(j*theta_n(t)). Everything else needed is there: multiple BSs in the 38.901 UMi/UMa/RMa/InH/InF scenarios (bs_loc/num_bs, Rel-19 v19_2 parameter files), multi-TX ResourceGrid/StreamManagement, a generic PilotPattern (SRS-like comb pilots can be built from it), LS/LMMSE OFDM channel estimators, RZF/CBF precoders (sionna.phy.ofdm.precoding), and Sionna RT for site-specific scenes. The NR module covers PUSCH only. There is no PDSCH, SRS, CSI-RS or TRS, so the downlink CJT chain is built from the generic OFDM blocks.

Kill test already run (numpy on CPU, 7 cases in about 1.5 minutes). Setup: N=4 single-antenna TRPs, static UE, SRS-based reciprocity, latency D = 4 slots. Without a tracking loop (always use the latest SRS phase), the coherent gain falls to the non-coherent level (about -6 dB for N=4) whenever relative CFO x (SRS period + latency) exceeds about 0.3 cycles. At the 3GPP +/-50 ppb bound this already happens at FR1 with a 5 ms SRS period: 103 deg rms error, and 2-UE ZF reaches only 0.27 of ideal-ZF rate.

With a second-order alpha-beta loop (equivalent to a type-II digital PLL) and a coarse CFO starting estimate, the loss shrinks to 0.01-0.07 dB of coherent gain. Measured: FR1 3.5 GHz, 5 ms SRS, 4 deg rms, ZF rate ratio 0.99. FR3 13 GHz, 5 ms SRS, 6.5 deg, 0.96. FR2 28 GHz, 2.5 ms SRS, 10 deg, 0.89. This holds even for free-running +/-2 ppm TCXOs, as on a USRP B210 (FR1: 4 deg rms, ZF rate 0.99).

Where the loop breaks: long SRS periods. At 80 ms (FR1, +/-2 ppb) the loop gets 37.6 deg rms (-0.67 dB), worse than no loop on that rms number. With noisier XO-class oscillators at 13 GHz and a 20 ms SRS period it gets 31 deg, ZF ratio 0.70. The cause is cycle slips: the frequency estimate is ambiguous beyond +/-1/(2*T_SRS). The loop needs a separate frequency-acquisition step, for example two DMRS/TRS symbols about 0.25 ms apart (unambiguous to about +/-2 kHz). Averaging the starting CFO estimate over 16 slots fixed the 20 ms cases (FR1 3.8 deg; FR3 13 GHz 6.9-7.1 deg) but not 80 ms.

Once the loop runs, the remaining error at FR2/FR3 comes from each radio's own synthesizer PLL jitter, which no slot-rate loop can remove. I modelled it as 1 deg rms at 3.5 GHz (the X310 datasheet value), scaled with carrier frequency. That puts an ideal-loop floor of about 10 deg relative error at 28 GHz, which gives ZF rate 0.89. So there is a measurable crossover carrier frequency where the bottleneck moves from tracking (software) to synthesizer phase noise (PLL hardware). This connects directly to your interest in PLLs.

The GPU is incidental for the loop itself. Pooling SRS phases across all UEs and ports costs about 10% of SRS channel estimation. Applying the correction to existing beamforming weights (diag(e^{-j theta}) x W) costs 0.003-18 MFLOP per slot: 0.28 GFLOP/s for 4 TRPs x 4 antennas and 4.5 GFLOP/s for 64 ports. The GPU is needed for the PHY around the loop. At cell-free scale (64 ports, 100 MHz, 16 layers, 48 SRS UEs per slot): SRS estimation about 443 GFLOP/s, RZF recompute every slot about 161 GFLOP/s, PDSCH precoding about 751 GFLOP/s. At 256 ports with a 0.25 ms slot this reaches about 4.7-12 TFLOP/s. NVIDIA Aerial cuPHY 26.3 already does SRS estimation plus RZF beamforming-weight calculation for 64T64R on GPU. The defensible GPU contribution is to fuse the per-TRP oscillator tracker into the SRS->BFW pipeline, pooled across all UEs, with no extra latency. The GPU is not what makes the loop possible.

Where intra-slot CFO correction can run depends on the split. With an O-RAN 7.2x split the GPU sees frequency-domain IQ only, so it can only apply per-symbol phase correction. That is fine if the residual offset is much smaller than the subcarrier spacing: 50 ppb at 3.5 GHz is 175 Hz, giving an ICI SIR of about 40 dB at 30 kHz. A free-running +/-2 ppm crystal is 7 kHz (ICI SIR about 12 dB) and needs time-domain correction in the RU or FPGA. On a USRP this is the FPGA DUC/DDC NCO, set through UHD tune_request dsp_freq.

Hardware choice: USRP B210 is the right kit. $2,387 each; ±2 ppm internal VCTCXO; AD9361; USB3. Its two channels share one TX LO and one RX LO, so one B210 is one TRP, not two. The X310 costs $11,462 plus $2,645 per UBX-160 (about $16k per unit). Its two daughterboards have separate LOs but share one reference, so they are not independent oscillators. Minimum rig: 2 TX B210s plus 1 RX B210, each with clock_source and time_source internal. Open each device as a separate multi_usrp, not one multi-device multi_usrp, which assumes a shared reference. Do not retune during a run: the AD9361 TX and RX LO phases re-randomise on each tune, which also breaks TX/RX reciprocity calibration. On B210 the sample clock and the LO come from the same crystal, so SFO in ppm equals CFO in ppm. Use short bursts (2 ppm x 10 ms = 20 ns) or narrowband pilots of 1 MHz or less, or resample.

Software: UHD 4.x Python API plus numpy or Sionna is enough. Merlo et al. used UHD 4.8 and GNU Radio 3.10 on X310s. OAI and srsRAN do not implement multi-TRP CJT with independent radios; in OAI multi-USRP setups expect a shared 10 MHz/PPS. A full-stack 5G CJT demo is out of MSc scope. Run at PHY level with NR numerology: 30 kHz SCS, comb-4 SRS-like pilots, 2-symbol DMRS-like frequency acquisition.

Over-the-air or cabled metrics: (a) coherent combining gain Gc = P(simultaneous TX) / sum(P_i individual). Ideal is N, i.e. 3 dB for 2 TX; the non-coherent mean is 0 dB. (b) Relative-phase residual rms vs prediction horizon (SRS period plus latency). (c) The most sensitive one: ZF null depth at a second RX. Leakage is roughly sigma^2, so 10 deg rms error gives about -15 dB nulls, while coherent gain at 10 deg is only about -0.1 dB. Close prior art shows these are measurable: Merlo et al. reported median coherent gain of 99% with incoherent clocks on X310s; RFClock combined 4 B210 TX coherently and measured B210 internal CFO of 75-350 Hz at 915 MHz.

what_is_already_solved: Over-the-air time, frequency and phase alignment of distributed radios with independent clocks has been demonstrated on SDRs several times: Quitin/Madhow 2013, USRP2 with an EKF frequency lock plus 1-bit feedback; MegaMIMO and AirShare (MIT); RFClock (B210, 4 coherent TX); Merlo/Nanzer 2025 (X310s, 60-70 ps, 99% median coherent gain, <5 ppb beamforming-frequency RMSE).

TDD distributed MIMO with over-the-air phase calibration built into the slot flow, for independent LOs: Ngo & Larsson, arXiv 2509.03722. COTS RRU cell-free with OTA reciprocity calibration and phase synchronisation: Cao et al., arXiv 2208.14048. mmWave cell-free bidirectional phase-coherent transmission and sensing prototype: Jiang et al., arXiv 2601.14648.

3GPP Rel-19 CJT calibration (CJTC): the UE measures and reports per-TRP frequency and phase offsets, so pre-compensating TRP frequency and phase for CJT is now in the standard (see the sibling Rel-19 notes in /tmp/.../phasesync/rel19*.txt).

The loop itself is textbook: a second-order PI/type-II DPLL or 2-state Kalman on SRS phase. Simulations of how sync offsets hurt distributed MIMO also exist, e.g. Bondada, Jakubisin & Buehrer, arXiv 2503.24314.
GPU SRS channel estimation plus RZF dynamic beamforming weights at 64T64R scale is already in NVIDIA Aerial cuPHY (26.3).
what_is_open: What real hardware does over the time horizons that matter. Relative-phase traces between independent cheap oscillators (B210 TCXOs) at 1-100 ms, fed through the loop, give residual error vs SRS period and latency. Most papers report a single operating point, not the trade-off curve.

Where the bottleneck moves from software to hardware: the carrier frequency (FR1 -> FR3 7-24 GHz -> FR2) at which the error after an ideal slot-rate loop is set by synthesizer integrated jitter. This tells you whether 6G FR3 CJT needs better PLLs or better tracking, and it ties straight to the PLL interest.

Pooling across UEs: the TRP oscillator term is common to every UE's SRS, while UE Doppler and channel change are per-UE. A GPU estimator that pools all UEs, ports and REs each slot could separate TRP drift from UE motion and allow longer SRS periods. I have not tested this; mobility was not modelled.
Cycle-slip-free frequency acquisition and tracking at long SRS periods (>=40-80 ms) and with XO-class oscillators at FR3. The simple loop failed here.
Interaction with TX/RX reciprocity calibration drift (AD9361 TX and RX LOs are separate synthesizers) and with SFO when the sample clock and LO share one free-running crystal.
implications: Recommended MSc framing: not "invent a PLL that fixes CJT", which Rel-19 CJTC, Ngo & Larsson and Merlo already cover. Instead: "measure and model the residual phase error of a GPU-pipelined distributed tracking loop vs SRS period, latency and carrier frequency, using real oscillator traces from independent SDRs, and find where synthesizer PLL jitter becomes the limit for FR3/6G CJT". That is specific, provable and honest about prior art.

Stage 0 (done, $0, minutes): killtest.py. It shows the effect is large (-6 dB at N=4 with no tracking) and that a simple loop recovers it at FR1/FR3 with SRS <=20 ms. Caveat: the no-loop baseline is a straw man, because real gNBs track CFO.

Stage 1, the real cheapest kill test (1-2 days, about $0-300 if the lab has 3 B210s). Rig: 2 TX B210s (internal clocks) plus 1 RX B210, cabled through attenuators and a combiner at 2.4 or 3.5 GHz, all on one host with UHD Python. The two TX alternate narrowband (<=1 MHz) pilot bursts every 0.5 ms for about 60 minutes, with no retuning. The RX LO cancels when you take the difference, so the RX gives the true relative phase trace psi(t). Replay the trace offline through the loop for SRS periods of 1-160 slots and latencies of 2-8 slots, and report residual rms and predicted coherent gain and null depth. Kill criteria: if the residual is under about 5 deg at all realistic periods at FR1 (as predicted), FR1 is solved and the project moves to FR3, multi-UE pooling or long periods. If real traces show much more than the model (temperature transients, B210 VCTCXO tuning steps), that excess is the research result.

Stage 2 (2-4 weeks): close the loop on hardware. The RX feeds psi-hat and f-hat back over Ethernet, TX2 pre-rotates through the UHD DSP NCO or digitally, both transmit together, and you measure Gc against the ideal 3 dB and ZF null depth at a second RX. Optional OTA run indoors in ISM or under an Ofcom innovation/trial licence.

Stage 3 (Sionna, about 2-10 GPU-h, $1-15) with the exact setup below. Scenario: 38.901 UMi or InH (v19_2), N in {2,4,8} TRPs x 4 antennas, K in {1,2,4} UEs. Numerology: 30 kHz SCS at 3.5 and 7 GHz, 60 kHz at 13 GHz, 120 kHz at 28 GHz. Oscillator model: two-state (theta, y), offset ±{2, 15, 50} ppb and ±2 ppm, WFM/RWFM fitted to the measured B210 ADEV, plus per-symbol white PM from PLL datasheets. Pilots: comb-4 single-symbol SRS at periods {2..160} slots, plus a 2-symbol DMRS/TRS for acquisition. Estimator: per-port LS, then pooled per-TRP common phase angle(sum conj(H_prev) H_now) relative to a reference TRP. Loop options: PI/alpha-beta vs 2-state Kalman vs none, with a loop-bandwidth sweep. Precoder: RZF per SRS with per-slot diagonal phase correction. Metrics: coherent-gain efficiency, SINR CDF, sum rate, null depth, BLER using the sionna.phy.fec LDPC chain.

Position the GPU honestly. It is required for the surrounding PHY at cell-free scale (hundreds of GFLOP/s to TFLOP/s) and for Monte-Carlo sweeps. The contribution is fusing pooled multi-UE oscillator tracking into the SRS->BFW GPU pipeline, for example as a cuPHY-style kernel or a Sionna/PyTorch module, with a latency measurement. The loop is not a GPU-only computation, and you should not claim it is.
red_flags: Heavy prior art: Rel-19 CJTC, Ngo & Larsson 2025-26, Merlo/Nanzer 2025, RFClock, MegaMIMO/AirShare, Quitin/Madhow 2013, Cao 2022, Jiang 2026. A plain "digital PLL across radios" is not novel. The novelty has to be the measured trade-off, FR3/PLL-floor analysis, or multi-UE pooled GPU tracking.

The dramatic -6 dB no-loop result is a straw man. Commercial TDD CJT already tracks frequency, and a tight PTP/SyncE cluster (±2 ppb) at FR1 with 5 ms SRS loses only 0.05 dB with no tracking at all. The real problem appears only at FR3/FR2, long SRS periods or loose frequency sync.

My simulation is simplified: single antenna per TRP, static UE, no SFO or timing error, perfect reciprocity calibration, white PM scaled linearly with fc, a crude alpha-beta grid (not an optimal Kalman), and oscillator noise coefficients (a_wfm=7.5e-13, b_rwfm=1e-10) that are assumed rather than measured. The cycle-slip failures partly reflect my crude coarse-CFO starting step.
The GPU is not necessary for the loop; claiming that would be overselling. For a 4-radio testbed a CPU handles everything (under 1.1 GFLOP/s).

USRP pitfalls: B210 channels share LOs (one TRP per B210). X310 daughterboards share one reference. AD9361 LO phase re-randomises on retune. Free-running sample clocks drift 2 us/s at 2 ppm, beyond the 2.3 us CP at 30 kHz within about 1 s unless resampled or burst-retimed. Without PPS, device times are offset by host latency. OTA work needs ISM bands or a licence; cabled is cleaner for the kill test.
Lab USRPs are unconfirmed. Without them the hardware stages cost about $7k (3x B210), and only the numpy/Sionna stages are $0-15.
OAI and srsRAN cannot run multi-TRP CJT with independent radios, so this will not be a full 5G-stack demo within an MSc timeline.
